(Benefit)

In Surah al-Insan, Allah mentions the reward of the righteous (al-abrar), while alerting to what is higher and more exalted than it, namely the reward of those brought near (al-muqarrabun), the foremost (al-sabiqun). This is to show that if this is the reward of the righteous who are moderate (al-muqtasidun), then what can be imagined of the reward of those brought near, the foremost? Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾

up to His saying:

﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups of crystal, crystal made of silver﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ [al-Insan: 5-21].

So here he mentioned bracelets of silver and cups of silver in the reward of the righteous.

(A Noble Principle)

A verb that takes complements through several different prepositions must not have, with each preposition, a meaning beyond the meaning of that preposition. This depends on how the meanings of the prepositions differ. If the two prepositions clearly differ, the difference becomes apparent, as in: raghibtu 'anhu and raghibtu fīhi, 'adaltu ilayhi and 'adaltu 'anhu, māltu ilayhi and 'anhu, sa'aytu ilayhi and sa'aytu bihi. If the meanings of the particles are close, the difference is hard to distinguish, as in: qaṣadtu ilayhi and qaṣadtu lahu, and hadaytuhu ila kadhā and hadaytuhu li-kadhā. The superficial grammarians (al-nuḥāh al-ẓāhiriyya) make one of the two prepositions carry the meaning of the other.

As for the jurists of Arabic (fuqahā' ahl al-'arabiyya), they do not accept this method. Rather, they give the verb a meaning with one preposition and a meaning with another, so they look at the preposition and what verbs it calls for, and they make the verb that takes it carry its meaning. This is the method of the master of the craft, Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, and the method of the skilled among his companions: they make the verb include the meaning of another verb, and they do not put one preposition in the place of another. This is a noble principle of great value, requiring insight and subtlety of mind. An example is God's words: ﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾. They make yashrabu (drinks) include the meaning of yarwā (quenches the thirst), so it takes the bāʾ that it requires. In this there is evidence for both verbs: one stated explicitly, and the other implied by the inclusion and indicated by the preposition that it requires, with extreme brevity.

This is among the wonders of the language, its beauties and its perfection.

This is better than saying yashrabu minhā, for that gives no indication of quenching, and better than saying yurwā bihā, for that does not indicate drinking by its explicit wording but only by implication. When He says ﴿yashrabu bihā﴾, it indicates drinking explicitly and quenching by the preposition bāʾ. So reflect on this.

He said in Ṭarīq al-Hijratayn:

He said: ﴿Drunk from by those brought near﴾, and did not say "minhā", indicating that their drinking is from the spring itself, purely, not from it and other things.

So yashrabu is made to include the meaning of yurwā, and so it takes bāʾ. This is more subtle in its derivation and better in meaning than to make bāʾ carry the meaning of min, rather the verb yashrabu includes the meaning of another verb and so is construed as that verb is. This is the method of the skilled among the grammarians, the method of Sibawayh and the leading figures among his companions.

He said in al-Abrār: ﴿They drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor﴾, because the drinking of those brought near is more perfect, so the bāʾ that indicates quenching by the spring, purely, is borrowed for it. The Qur'an's indication is subtler and more eloquent than humans can encompass.

He said in Ḥādī al-Arwāḥ:

The statement ﴿yashrabu bihā﴾ has been disputed. The Kufans said: the bāʾ means min, i.e., "drinks from it." Others said: rather, the verb includes the meaning of yashrabu "with it" (i.e., yurwā bihā, quenched by it), and since it includes its meaning, it takes its construction.

This is more correct, subtler and more eloquent.

A group said: the bāʾ indicates location, and ʿayn is a noun of place, as when you say "we were in such-and-such a place."

A parallel to this inclusion is God's words: ﴿Whoever intends therein wrongdoing by deviation﴾, where yurid includes the meaning of yahumm (intends), so it takes the construction of that verb.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger, a spring therein called Salsabil﴾. He informed that the spring from which those brought near drink purely, the drink of the righteous is mixed from it, because those people devoted all their deeds purely to God, so their drink was purified, while these were mixed, so their drink was mixed.

A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Indeed the righteous will be in bliss, upon couches they look on. You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss. They are given to drink of a sealed nectar, its seal is musk, and for this let those who compete compete. Its mixture is from Tasnīm, a spring from which those brought near drink﴾.

He informed, exalted is He, about the mixture of their drink with two things: camphor at the beginning of the sūrah and ginger at its end. In camphor there is coolness and good fragrance, and in ginger there is warmth and good fragrance, which produce for them, through the combining of the two drinks, a further state more perfect, better and more delightful than each one alone, and balancing the quality of each with the quality of the other. How subtle is the placement of the mention of camphor at the beginning of the sūrah and ginger at its end: their drink is first mixed with camphor, which contains coolness, and then ginger follows and balances it.

It is apparent that the second cup is other than the first, and that they are two delightful kinds of drink: one mixed with camphor, the other mixed with ginger.

Furthermore, He, exalted is He, informed about the mixing of their drink with camphor and its coolness, in contrast to what He described them with: the heat of fear, preference (of others), patience, and fulfilment of all obligations, of which He pointed out the fulfilment of the lesser, namely what they obligated upon themselves by vow, as an indication of fulfilling the greater, namely what God obligated upon them. For this reason He said: ﴿And He rewarded them for what they endured with a garden and silk﴾.

For in patience there is roughness and restraining the soul from its desires, which required that their reward include the spaciousness of the garden and the softness of silk, which correspond to that restraint and roughness, and combined for them freshness and joy. This is the beauty of their outward state, and this is the condition of their inward state, just as in this world they adorned their outward with the laws of Islam and their inward with the realities of faith.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verse 8–9:

And in the hadith of Mu'adh, from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Charity extinguishes sin just as water extinguishes fire."

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from the hadith of Abu Yusuf al-Qadi, from al-Mukhtar ibn Fulful, from Anas, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Hasten with charity, for calamity does not overtake charity."

In the Two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"When a servant gives charity from lawful earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, Allah takes it in His right hand and nurtures it for one of them, just as one of you nurtures his foal or his young camel, until a date becomes like a great mountain."

In the wording of al-Bayhaqi for this hadith: "until a date or a morsel becomes greater than Uhud."

Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said:

"Among the things that bring forgiveness is feeding a hungry Muslim."

It has been narrated in a raised (marfu') form through more than one route.

If Allah, glorified is He, has forgiven one who gave water to a dog in its intense thirst, then how about one who gives drink to the thirsty, feeds the hungry, and clothes the naked among the Muslims?!

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Protect yourselves from the Fire, even with half a date; and if you cannot find it, then with a good word."

He made good words a substitute for charity for one who is unable to give it.

They said: Where is the pleasure of charity and benevolence, and their gladdening of the heart and strengthening of it, and what Allah, glorified is He, places for those who give charity of love and esteem in the hearts of His servants, prayers for them, praise of them, and bringing joy to them, along with the reward of patience in poverty?

Yes, indeed, there is a great reward for it, but rewards differ in rank with Allah.

They also said: Charity, benevolence and giving are attributes of the Lord, the Exalted, and the most beloved of His servants to Him are those who embody these qualities, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"The creation is the dependents of Allah, so the most beloved of creation to Him is the one most beneficial to His dependents."

They said: Allah, glorified is He, has mentioned the categories of the blessed and began with the givers of charity, first among them, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who lend to Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward. And those who believed in Allah and His messengers — those are the truthful ones (al-siddiqun) and the martyrs with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light.﴾

So these are the categories of the blessed, and foremost among them are the male givers of charity and the female givers of charity.

They said: In charity there are benefits and advantages that none can count except Allah.

(A subtle point)

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not want from you reward or thanks.﴾

He made the ultimate aim of the deeds of the righteous, the near ones, and the lovers: seeking His countenance.

(A caution)

Some scholars mentioned, regarding the saying of Allah ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ up to His saying ﴿They fulfill vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread. And they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾, that what is meant by this is ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him).

Thus, along with carrying this general wording, he combined an open lie and fabrication in claiming its revelation concerning ʿAli, for the surah is Meccan, and ʿAli was in Mecca, poor, raised by the Prophet in his care.

When Abu Talib died, the sons of ʿAbd al-Muttalib divided his children, since he had no wealth; so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took ʿAli, raised him with himself, and included him in his household, so he was among them.

(A benefit)

The verbal noun (masdar), in its strict sense, is not pluralized, because all masdars are of one genus in that they express the action of the agent, and an action resembles another action and does not differ from it in its essence. Were it not for the feminine ending (ta' marbuta) in ḥaraka, its pluralization would not be permissible. So if the Arabs had uttered a masdar such as ḥilm (forbearance) — and they have dispensed with it by ḥilm — or a masdar such as shukr (thanks) — and they have dispensed with it by shukr — it would not be permissible to pluralize it, because difference of types does not return to it; rather it returns to the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq). Do you not see that shukr is an expression of what is repaid to the benefactor, whether in praise or action, and likewise its opposite, kufr, is an expression of what is confronted with the benefactor, whether denial or ugly conduct? So it is an absolute object, not a masdar from which the verb is derived. However, kufr is transitive with the preposition bi- because it implies the meaning of denial, while shakara is transitive with the preposition li-, the preposition of attribution, because the thing actually thanked is the favor, which is attributed to the benefactor; likewise the thing actually denied is the favor, but its denial is denial and rejection. Hence they say kafara bi-llah, kafara ni'matahu, shakara lahu, and shakara ni'matahu. And when it is established that shukr, from your saying shakartu shukran, is an absolute object, and it is of differing types because repayments for favors differ, it is permissible for it to be pluralized, just as ḥilm and shughl were pluralized.

So His saying, glorified is He, reporting about His sincere servants: ﴿We do not want from you reward or thanks﴾ may be a plural of shukr, and it is not like qu'ud and julus, because it is transitive, and the masdar of a transitive verb does not come in the pattern fu'ul.

I say: The correct view is that it is a masdar that came in the pattern fu'ul, because its opposites, kufr, juhud and nufur, have their masdars in the pattern fu'ul, such as kufur, juhud and nufur. It is utterly far-fetched that kafur be meant as a plural of kufr, and kufr is never known to be pluralized in the Qur'an or in usage; one does not know in speech kuffar or kufur. What is known is kufr, kufran and kufur, which are masdars and nothing else.

So the coming of shukur in the pattern fu'ul is fitting when it is understood by analogy with its opposite, and this is common in the language, and the indication of it has already been given. And even if shukur were permissible to use as a plural and could carry both the plural and the masdar meaning, the masdar would be more suitable to the meaning of the verse than the plural, because Allah, the Exalted, described them as sincere and that they intended by feeding food only His countenance and did not seek from those they fed reward or thanks. It is not fitting in this context to say "we do not want from you kinds of thanks and types of it"; rather, what is most fitting for them and their sincerity is to say "we do not want from you thanks at all," thereby negating from them the desire for this very reality, and this is more eloquent in expressing sincere intention than negating types. Consider it.

It is evident, so the verse fits only the masdar.

Likewise His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For whoever wishes to remember, or wishes gratitude (shukur)﴾ is only a masdar, and it is not the well-known clear pluralization of shukr as shukur, nor its usage in that way, just as, if this were not known for kufur, one would dispense with the absolute object in place of the masdar.

(A benefit)

Whoever gives himself latitude in following desire, Allah constricts his grave and his Day of return for him.

And whoever constricts himself by opposing desire, Allah widens it for him in his grave and his return.

Allah, the Exalted, has indicated this in His saying: ﴿And He will reward them for what they endured with a garden and silk﴾.

Because patience, which is restraining the self from desire, contains roughness and constriction, He recompensed them for it with the softness of silk and the vastness of the Garden.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding this verse: "He rewarded them for what they endured from desires."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verses 11–12:

He said concerning the people of Paradise: ﴿And He will give them radiance and joy. And will reward them for what they patiently endured with a garden and silk.﴾

So He made their faces radiant, their inner selves joyful, and their bodies clothed in silk. He, glorified is He, loves beauty in speech, actions, clothing and appearance, just as He hates ugliness in speech, actions, garments and appearance. So He hates the ugly and its people, and loves beauty and its people. However, two groups have gone astray on this subject. One group said: whatever He has created is beautiful, He loves everything He has created, and we love all that He has created, so we do not hate anything of it. They said: whoever sees existing things with His eye sees them all as beautiful. And their poet recited:

"When you see existing things with their eyes, all that existence contains is lovely."

They argued with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who perfected everything He created﴾, and His saying: ﴿The handiwork of God, who has perfected everything﴾, and His saying: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no imbalance﴾.

The "knower" (al-'arif) among them is the one who openly affirms the absoluteness of beauty and sees nothing ugly in existence. These people have lost zeal for God from their hearts, as well as hatred for the sake of God, enmity for His sake, forbidding wrong, striving in His way, and upholding His limits. They see the beauty of forms, male and female, as part of the beauty that God loves, and so they worship through their sinfulness. Some of them go to such extremes that one claims his object of worship appears in that form and dwells within it; and if he is a monist (ittihadi), he says that it is a manifestation of the Truth, and calls them "the aesthetic manifestations."

(Section)

Nadrah is the delight and goodliness that the face is clothed with from the traces of faith, the inner self's joy in it, the heart's gladness and its pleasure in it. This delight, joy and happiness then appear as radiance on the face. For this reason, He, glorified is He, combines delight, joy and radiance, as in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So God protected them from the evil of that day and gave them radiance and joy.﴾

So radiance is in their faces and joy is in their hearts. Bliss and the goodness of the heart manifest as radiance in the face, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss.﴾

(Benefit)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He will give them radiance and joy.﴾

So radiance is the beauty of faces, and joy is the beauty of hearts.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verse 13:

As for al-arā'ik (the couches), it is the plural of arīka. Mujahid related from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Reclining therein on couches﴾

He said: An arīka is not an arīka until there is a bed (sarīr) within a hujla (canopied enclosure).

So if there is a bed without a hujla, it is not an arīka.

And if there is a hujla without a bed, it is not an arīka either. An arīka is only an arīka when the bed is within the hujla, and when the two are combined, it is an arīka.

Mujahid also said: They are the beds within the hujal (canopied enclosures).

Al-Layth said: The arīka is a bed within a hujla, so the hujla and the bed together are an arīka, and its plural is arā'ik.

Abu Ishaq said: The arā'ik are the furnishings within the hujal.

I say: Here there are three things. The first is the bed (sarīr).

The second is the hujla, which is the canopy (bushkhana) hung above it.

The third is the bedding (firāsh) that is on the bed. The bed is not called an arīka until all of that is combined.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): The arīka is a decorated bed prepared in a dome or a room. If there is no bed in it, it is a hujla, and the plural is arā'ik.

In a hadith: "The seal of the Prophet ﷺ was like the button (zirr) of the hujla."

It is the button that joins its two sides, one of its buttons. And Allah knows best.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "When he wishes to take from its fruit, it lowers itself to him until he takes what he desires."

Another said: "Near to them, made easy, however they wish. They take from them standing, sitting, and reclining, which is like His saying: ﴿Its fruits hang low, within reach﴾."

The meaning of tadhlil al-qatf (the subjugation of the fruit-cluster) is making it easy to take. The people of Madina say dhalla al-nakhl, meaning he smoothed its roots and extracted it from the palm fronds, so that it becomes easy to reach.

As for the accusative of (dāniyatan) there are two opinions:

The first: it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), coordinated with His saying (muttakiʾīna) ["reclining"].

The second: it is an adjective (ṣifa) of the Garden.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verse 15:

"Qawarir" are glass vessels. He, glorified and exalted is He, informed us about the material of those vessels: that they are of silver, and that they have the clarity and transparency of glass. This is among the finest and most wondrous of things. He, glorified and exalted is He, cut off the supposition that those qawarir are of glass, saying: ﴿Qawarira min fiddah﴾ (Crystal-clear vessels of silver).

Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Kalbi and al-Sha'bi said: The qawarir of Paradise are of silver, so there combines in them the whiteness of silver and the clarity of crystal.

Ibn Qutaybah said: Everything in Paradise, including its rivers, its couches, its furnishings and its cups, differs from what is made by human craftsmanship in the world, as Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is nothing in the world of what is in Paradise except the names."

Cups in the world may be made of silver and may be made of glass, so God informed us that there are cups in Paradise which have the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.

He said: This is by way of simile; He meant qawarir as if they were made of silver. This is like His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿As if they were the hyacinth and the coral﴾ (Qur'an 55:58).

That is, they have the colours of coral with the clarity of hyacinth. This view is rejected, for the verse is explicit that they are of silver. The "min" here indicates the kind (min li-bayan al-jins), as when you say, "a ring of silver" (khatam min fiddah), and it is not meant that it resembles silver, but that its kind and material is silver. Perhaps he was troubled by the fact that they are of silver yet are qawarir, which is glass; but there is no difficulty in that, for the reason we have mentioned.

As for His saying ﴿qaddarūhā taqdīrā﴾ (they have measured them with a [precise] measure): taqdir means making a thing according to a specific measure. So the craftsmen fashioned these vessels according to the measure of their thirst, neither exceeding it nor falling short of it. This is more eloquent in terms of the drinker's pleasure: if it fell short of his thirst, his enjoyment would diminish, and if it exceeded it to the point of repulsion, he would become weary and bored with what remained.

This is the view of a group of exegetes.

Al-Farra' said: They measured the cup according to the measure of each one's thirst, with no excess and no deficiency, and it is the most delicious of drinks.

Al-Zajjaj said: They made the vessel according to the amount they need and desire.

Abu 'Ubayd said: The taqdir is that those who serve them measure them and then give them to drink.

He means that the pronoun in (qaddarū) refers to the angels and the servants, who measured the cup according to the measure of quenching thirst, so that it is not so much as to weigh down the hand, nor so little as to fall short.

Then the soul seeks more, as previously mentioned.

Another group said: The pronoun refers to the drinkers, meaning: they determined in themselves something, and what came to them corresponded to what they had determined and desired.

The view of the majority is better and more eloquent, and it entails this view as well, and God knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verse 17:

A group said: "Salsabeelan" is a compound sentence made of a verb and a subject, with "salsabeelan" in the accusative as an object, meaning "ask for a path to it (sal sabeelan ilayha)." But this is not correct. Rather, "salsabeel" is a single word and is the name of the spring itself, considered in terms of its quality. Qatada and Mujahid have indeed given a satisfying account of the derivation of the word.

Qatada said: it is "salsa," meaning they direct it wherever they wish. This is from the greater derivation (al-ishtiqaq al-akbar).

Mujahid said: "salsah al-sayl" means the flowing of the water is smooth and its current is sharp.

Abu al-Aliyah said: "al-muqabilan" means it flows over them in the roads and in their dwellings, and this is from its smoothness and the unity of its flow.

Others said: its meaning is good taste and savour.

Abu Ishaq said: "Salsabeel" is an adjective for something that is extremely smooth, so the spring was named by it.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "The correct view regarding Salsabeel is that it is an adjective for the water, and not the name of the spring. He argued for this with two proofs. The first: Salsabeel is declined (munsarif), and if it were the name of the spring it would not be declined, because of the feminine form and definiteness (al-ta'nith wa al-'alamiyyah). The second: Ibn Abbas said: its meaning is that it slides down into their throats with ease."

I say: he has no proof in either of them. As for the declension, it is required by the rhyme endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayat), as is the case with its parallels. As for the statement of Ibn Abbas, it only indicates that the spring was named by reference to the quality of smoothness and ease.

(Section)

Abu Nu'aym mentioned in the book "al-Tibb al-Nabawi" from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

"The king of the Romans sent a jar of ginger as a gift to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he fed each person a piece, and fed me a piece."

Ginger is hot in the second degree and moist in the first degree; it warms, aids the digestion of food, and is moderately laxative of the belly. It is beneficial for blockages of the liver arising from cold and moisture, and for dimness of sight arising from moisture, whether eaten or applied as a collyrium. It aids sexual intercourse, and it dissolves the thick winds that arise in the intestines and stomach.

In sum, it is suitable for a liver and stomach of cold temperament. When taken with sugar, two dirhams by weight in hot water, it purges viscous, phlegmatic humours, and it enters into compound electuaries that dissolve and melt phlegm.

Its candied (mizzi) form is hot and dry; it stimulates sexual desire, increases semen, warms the stomach and liver, aids digestion, dries up the predominant phlegm in the body, increases memory, suits the coldness of the liver and stomach, removes the dampness arising from eating fruit, sweetens the breath, and repels the harm of thick, cold foods.

Ibn Qayyim's commentary on Surah 76, verse 19:

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Farra' said: "Mukhalladun" means they do not grow old, nor do they change.

He said: The Arabs say of a man who has aged but has not gone grey, "innahu lamukhallad" (he is ever-young), and if his teeth have not fallen out from old age, it is said, "huwa mukhallad."

Others said: "Mukhalladun" means "muqarrat"un musawwarun," i.e., there are earrings in their ears and bracelets on their wrists.

This is the view preferred by Ibn al-A'rabi, who said: "Mukhalladun muqarratun bil-khalda," and its plural is khald, which are earrings. 

Amr narrated from his father: "khallada jariyatahu" means he adorned his slave-girl with khald, which are earrings; and "khalad" means he has aged but not turned grey. Likewise Sa'id ibn Jubayr said "muqarratun."

Those who held this view argued with two proofs:

The first: that immortality (khulud) is general to everyone who enters Paradise, so the young boys must be described with a particular immortality, and that is the earrings.

The second proof is the saying of the poet:

"And adorned women with silver, as if their buttocks were still dunes of sand."

The first group said: "Al-khuld" is remaining (baqa'). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Boys who do not die."

And the word of the interpreter of the Qur'an on this is sufficient.

This is also the view of Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, who said: they do not grow old, nor do they decline, nor do they change.

A group combined the two views and said: they are young boys to whom old age and decrepitude do not come, and in their ears are earrings.

Whoever says "muqarratun" means this meaning: that being young boys is a permanent condition for them.

God, glorified is He, likened them to scattered pearls because of their whiteness and beautiful form.

In their being scattered there are two benefits:

The first: indicating that they are not idle, but dispersed in their service and their needs.

The second: that pearls, when scattered, especially on a carpet of gold or silk, are more beautiful in appearance and more splendid than when gathered in one place.

It has been disputed whether these young boys are the young boys of this world or whether God created them anew in Paradise, on two views.

Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Hasan al-Basri said: they are the children of the Muslims who die having neither good deeds nor bad deeds; they will be the servants of the people of Paradise and their attendants, since Paradise has no procreation.

Al-Hakim said: Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hasan told us, Ibrahim ibn al-Husayn told us, Adam told us, al-Mubarak ibn Fadala told us, from al-Hasan regarding His words (wildan mukhalladun): He said: they had no good deeds nor bad deeds for which they would be punished, so they were placed in this position.

Among the adherents of this view are those who said they are the children of polytheists, whom God made servants for the people of Paradise.

These people argued with what Ya'qub ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Fari narrated from Abu Hazim, who said: al-Madini said, from Yazid al-Raqqashi, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"I asked my Lord that the innocent ones (al-lahin) among the offspring of mankind not be punished, and He gave them to me, so they are the servants of the people of Paradise."

Meaning the children. Al-Daraqutni said: it was also narrated by Abd al-Aziz al-Majishun from Ibn al-Munkadir from Yazid al-Raqqashi from the Prophet (ﷺ). End of quote.

It was also narrated by Fudayl ibn Sulayman from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq from al-Zuhri from Anas.

These chains are weak: Yazid is worthless (wahin), Fudayl ibn Sulayman is criticised, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq is weak.

Ibn Qutayba said: "al-lahun" is from "lahiytu 'an al-shay'" when one is heedless of something, and it is not from "lahawtu."

The proponents of the first view do not say that these are children born to the people of Paradise in it; rather they say they are boys whom God created in Paradise, just as He created the Hur al-'In.

They said: As for the young boys of the people of this world, on the Day of Resurrection they will be thirty-three years old, as narrated by Ibn Wahb: Amr ibn al-Harith informed us that Darraj Abu al-Samh narrated to him from Abu al-Haytham from Abu Sa'id, who said the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"Whoever of the people of Paradise dies, young or old, will be returned at the age of thirty in Paradise, and they will not exceed it forever. And likewise the people of Hell."

Narrated by al-Tirmidhi.

The more likely view is that these young boys are created from Paradise, like the Hur al-'In, as servants for them and attendants, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And there will go round among them young boys made for them, as if they were pearls well-guarded﴾.

These are other than their children, for it is part of the completeness of God's honour to them that He makes their children served along with them, and does not make them their attendants.

It has already been mentioned in the hadith of Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"I will be the first of people to come forth when they are resurrected," and in it: "He will be attended by a thousand servants, as if they were pearls well-guarded."

Al-Maknun is that which is hidden, protected, which hands have not handled. If you reflect on the word "al-wildan" and the phrase "wa-yatufu 'alayhim," and compare them with His words "wa-yatufu 'alayhim ghilmanun lahum," and join that to the hadith of Abu Sa'id mentioned above, you will know that "al-wildan" are boys whom God created in Paradise as servants for its people. And God knows best.

**(Section: On the mention of the kingdom of Paradise, and that all its people are kings therein)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom.﴾

Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid regarding "a great kingdom," that he said: "Immense." He also said: "The seeking of permission by the angels: the angels do not enter upon them except with permission."

Ka'b said regarding the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom﴾:

"Their Lord sends to them the angels, and the angels come and seek permission to enter upon them, the angels."

Some of them said: "The servants (khadam). The angels do not enter upon them except with permission."

Al-Hakam ibn Aban related from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that he mentioned the mounts of the people of Paradise, then recited: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom.﴾

Ibn Abi al-Hawari said: I heard Abu Sulayman say regarding the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom.﴾ He said: "The great kingdom is that the messenger comes to him with a gift and a kindness, and he does not reach him until permission is sought for him to enter upon him. He says to the chamberlain (hajib): 'Seek permission for me to enter upon the friend of God, for I cannot reach him,' and that chamberlain informs another chamberlain, and another chamberlain after that. From his abode to the Abode of Peace (Dar al-Salam) there is a gate through which he enters upon his Lord whenever he wills, without permission. So the great kingdom is that the messenger of the Lord of Might does not enter upon him except with permission, while he enters upon his Lord without permission."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Salih ibn Malik narrated to us, Salih al-Murri narrated to us, Yazid al-Raqqashi narrated to us, from Anas ibn Malik, raising it (to the Prophet ﷺ): "Indeed, the lowest of all the people of Paradise in rank is the one over whose head stand ten thousand servants."

Muhammad ibn Abbad ibn Musa narrated to us: Zayd ibn al-Hubab informed us, from Abu Hilal al-Rasibi, Al-Hajjaj ibn Attab al-Abdi informed us, from Abd Allah ibn Ma'bad al-Zimmani, from Abu Hurayrah, who said:

"Indeed, the lowest of the people of Paradise in rank, and there is none base among them, has fifteen thousand servants who attend him every morning and evening, and no servant among them except that he has a rarity not possessed by his companion."

Muhammad ibn Abbad also narrated to me: Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, from Abu Hilal, Humayd ibn Hilal narrated to us, who said:

"There is no man of the people of Paradise except that he has a thousand treasurers, and none of them is a treasurer except over a task that his companion does not have."

Harun ibn Sufyan narrated to me: Muhammad ibn Umar informed us, al-Fadl ibn Fudalah informed us, from Zuhrah ibn Ma'bad, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli, who said:

"Indeed, when the servant first enters Paradise, seventy thousand servants meet him, as if they were pearls."

Harun ibn Sufyan narrated to me: Muhammad ibn Umar narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Hilal informed us, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said:

"Indeed, the lowest of the people of Paradise in rank, and there is none base among them, has ten thousand servants who attend him, with each servant a rarity not possessed by his companion."

Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: Yahya ibn Ayyub narrated to us, Abd Allah ibn Rajaz narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Abi Ayyub al-Makhzumi, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Maghafiri, who said:

"Indeed, there are set out for a man of the people of Paradise two rows of his young servants, whose ends cannot be seen; when he passes, they walk behind him."

Abu Khaythamah said: Al-Hasan ibn Musa narrated to us, Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, Darraj narrated to us, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed, the lowest of the people of Paradise in rank is the one who has eighty thousand servants, and seventy-two wives, and a dome of pearl, ruby and chrysolite is erected for him, as wide as the distance between al-Jabiyah and Sana'a."

Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid informed us, Arta'ah ibn al-Mundhir narrated to me, who said: I heard a man from the elders of the army, called Abu al-Hajjaj, say: I sat with Abu Umamah, and he said:

"Indeed, the believer, when he enters Paradise, will be reclining on a couch, and he has two rows of servants, and at the end of the two rows is a gate with a doorkeeper. An angel comes and seeks permission. The farthest of the servants says to the one next to him: 'An angel seeks permission.' The one next to him says: 'An angel seeks permission,' until it reaches the believer, and he says: 'Let him in.' The one closest to the believer says: 'Let him in,' and the one next to him says to the one next to him: 'Let him in,' until it reaches the farthest of them, who is at the gate, and he opens for him, and he enters and greets him, then he departs."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, Qabisah narrated to us, Qays ibn Sulaym al-Anbari narrated to us, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who said:

"While a friend of God, Mighty and Majestic, was in his abode, a messenger from God, Mighty and Majestic, came to him, and said to the doorkeeper: 'Seek permission for the messenger of God, Mighty and Majestic, to enter upon the friend of God.' The doorkeeper enters and says: 'O friend of God, this is a messenger from God, Mighty and Majestic, seeking permission.' He said: 'Let him in.' So he is admitted, and he enters upon God, Mighty and Majestic, and he places before Him a gift. Then He says: 'O friend of God, indeed your Lord sends you His greetings, and commands you to eat from this.' He (the friend) compares it to a food he had eaten just now. He says: 'I have only just eaten from this.' He says: 'Indeed your Lord commands you to eat from it.' So he eats from it, and finds in it the taste of every fruit in Paradise. That is the saying of Him, the Exalted: ﴿And they will be given it, resembling one another.﴾"

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verse 21:

So the bracelets adorned their outward appearances, and the pure drink purified their inner selves.

He said in (Hadi al-Arwah):

His saying ﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade, and they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾: this is the adornment of the outward.

Then he said ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾: this is the adornment of the inward, purified for them from every harm and deficiency.

(Section)

Consider what the word (ʿāliyahum) indicates: that this clothing is apparent and visible, adorning their outward appearance. It is not like an undergarment worn next to the body, but rather like that which is worn over garments for beauty and ornament.

The seven readers differed over the accusative (naṣb) and nominative (raf') of (ʿāliyahum), so there are two readings.

The grammarians differed over the grammatical basis of its accusative form: whether it is a circumstantial adverb of place (ẓarf) or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), giving two opinions.

The exegetes differed over whether this refers to the youths (wildān) who circulate among them, so that they circulate while wearing garments of green silk and brocade, or to the masters (sādāt) whom the youths serve, so that they circulate among their masters while the masters wear these garments. The ḥāl reading is not clear here, and it does not carry that wonderful, marvelous meaning.

The correct view is that it is accusative as an adverb of place, since (ʿāliyan), in the sense of (fawq, "above"), is treated as such. Abu ʿAli said: "This reading is clearer, namely that (ʿāliyan) is an adjective that has been used as an adverb, just as in His saying ﴿The riders are lower than you﴾ (al-rakb asfala minkum), and as they say: he is on the side of the house (huwa nāḥiyatun min al-dār)."

As for those who read (ʿāliyahum) in the nominative, it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) with (thiyāb sundus) as its predicate. The singular form (ʿāl) with the plural (thiyāb) does not prevent this, since the pattern (fāʿil) may be used to express plurality, as in the poet's words:

"Surely my neighbors this evening are departing ...
Called by desires of passion and longing."

And He, exalted, says: ﴿Arrogant about it, conversing by night, speaking evil﴾.

Whoever reads (khuḍran) in the nominative makes it an adjective of (thiyāb), and this is the more analogical on several grounds:

First: agreement between them in the plural.

Second: its conformity with His saying: ﴿and they will wear green garments﴾.

Third: it avoids describing a singular with a plural.

Whoever reads it in the genitive makes it an adjective of (sundus), taking it as a collective noun, as one says: "The yellow dinar and the white dirham have ruined people."

The first reading is also preferred on a fourth ground: the Arabs use a plural that is in the form of a singular and treat it as a singular, as in His saying: ﴿He who has made for you fire from the green tree﴾, and His saying ﴿as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾.

Since they have given the adjectives of this kind of plural singular form, giving the adjective of the singular form is even more appropriate, even if it carries the sense of the plural.

As for (istabraq), there are two readings: the nominative, in coordination with (thiyāb), and the genitive, in coordination with (sundus).

Consider how He combined for them the two kinds of outward adornment, clothing and jewelry, just as He combined for them the outward and the inward, as mentioned shortly before.

So He adorned their inner selves with the pure drink, their forearms with bracelets, and their bodies with silk garments.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verse 22:

He named Himself "Shākir" (the Appreciative) and "Shakūr" (the Most Appreciative), and He named those who give thanks by these two names. He granted them a share of His attribute and named them by His name. And that is sufficient as proof of His love for the grateful and of His favour toward them.

His calling the grateful servant "mashkūr" (one who is thanked) is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, this has been a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insan: 22].

The Lord's being pleased with His servant for his gratitude is like His saying: ﴿And if you are grateful, He is pleased with it for you﴾ [al-Zumar: 7]. And the scarcity of its people among the worlds indicates that they are His elite. Like His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13].

In the two Sahihs, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he stood (in prayer) until his feet swelled. It was said to him: "You do this, though Allah has forgiven you your earlier and later sins?" He said: "Shall I not be a grateful servant?"

And he said to Mu'adh: "By Allah, O Mu'adh, I love you. Do not forget to say at the end of every prayer: 'O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well.'"

(Qā'idah)

The servant has two standing-positions before Allah: a standing before Him in prayer, and a standing before Him on the day of meeting Him.

Whoever fulfils the rights of the first standing, the other standing will be made easy for him.

And whoever treats this standing lightly and does not give it its due, that standing will be made hard for him.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And during the night, prostrate yourself to Him and glorify Him through the long night. Indeed, these love the fleeting life and leave behind them a heavy Day.﴾

And opposing them in the second group, they said: Allah, glorified is He, has condemned the beauty of forms, the perfection of stature and physique. He said about the hypocrites: ﴿And when you see them, their bodies impress you﴾, and He said: ﴿And how many generations did We destroy before them who were better in furnishings and appearance?﴾

That is: in wealth and appearance. Al-Hasan said: it means forms.

In Sahih Muslim, from him (ﷺ):

"Indeed Allah does not look at your forms and your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

They said: It is known that He did not negate the sight of perception; rather He negated the sight of love.

They said: He has also forbidden us to wear silk and gold, and vessels of gold and silver, and that is among the greatest beauties of this world.

And He said: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given in enjoyment to pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world, that We may test them therein.﴾

And in a hadith: "Simplicity of dress is part of faith."

Allah has condemned the extravagant, and extravagance occurs in clothing just as it occurs in food and drink.

The resolution of the dispute is to say: beauty in form, clothing and appearance is of three kinds:

Some of it is praiseworthy, some of it is blameworthy, and some of it is neither praised nor blamed.

The praiseworthy is that which is for Allah's sake and helps obedience to Allah, implementing His commands and responding to Him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) would adorn himself for delegations; and it is comparable to the clothing of weapons for fighting, and to wearing silk in battle and the pride in it, for that is praiseworthy when it entails raising the word of Allah, supporting His religion, and enraging His enemy.

The blameworthy is that which is for worldly life, leadership, boasting, arrogance, and as a means to desires, and that it becomes the servant's ultimate aim and furthest goal; for many souls have no aspiration other than that.

As for what is neither praised nor blamed, it is that which is free of these two intentions and stripped of these two qualities.

The point is that this noble hadith, "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty," comprises two great principles: its beginning is knowledge (ma'rifah) and its end is conduct (sulūk). So He is known, glorified is He, by the beauty to which nothing is comparable, and He is worshipped by the beauty He loves in words, deeds and character. He loves that His servant beautify his tongue with truthfulness, his heart with sincerity, love, turning back (to Him) and reliance, his limbs with obedience, and his body by displaying His blessings upon him in his clothing, and by purifying it of impurities, ritual impurities, filth, unwanted hair, what is disliked, circumcision and trimming the nails. So He is known by attributes of beauty, and He makes Himself known through beautiful deeds, words and character; thus He is known by the beauty that is His attribute, and worshipped by the beauty that is His law and religion.

Thus the hadith combines the two principles: knowledge and conduct.

(Qā'idah)

The servant has two standing-positions before Allah: a standing before Him in prayer, and a standing before Him on the day of meeting Him.

Whoever fulfils the rights of the first standing, the other standing will be made easy for him.

And whoever treats this standing lightly and does not give it its due, that standing will be made hard for him.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And during the night, prostrate yourself to Him and glorify Him through the long night. Indeed, these love the fleeting life and leave behind them a heavy Day.﴾

And opposing them in the second group, they said: Allah, glorified is He, has condemned the beauty of forms, the perfection of stature and physique. He said about the hypocrites: ﴿And when you see them, their bodies impress you﴾, and He said: ﴿And how many generations did We destroy before them who were better in furnishings and appearance?﴾

That is: in wealth and appearance. Al-Hasan said: it means forms.

In Sahih Muslim, from him (ﷺ):

"Indeed Allah does not look at your forms and your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

They said: It is known that He did not negate the sight of perception; rather He negated the sight of love.

They said: He has also forbidden us to wear silk and gold, and vessels of gold and silver, and that is among the greatest beauties of this world.

And He said: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given in enjoyment to pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world, that We may test them therein.﴾

And in a hadith: "Simplicity of dress is part of faith."

Allah has condemned the extravagant, and extravagance occurs in clothing just as it occurs in food and drink.

The resolution of the dispute is to say: beauty in form, clothing and appearance is of three kinds:

Some of it is praiseworthy, some of it is blameworthy, and some of it is neither praised nor blamed.

The praiseworthy is that which is for Allah's sake and helps obedience to Allah, implementing His commands and responding to Him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) would adorn himself for delegations; and it is comparable to the clothing of weapons for fighting, and to wearing silk in battle and the pride in it, for that is praiseworthy when it entails raising the word of Allah, supporting His religion, and enraging His enemy.

The blameworthy is that which is for worldly life, leadership, boasting, arrogance, and as a means to desires, and that it becomes the servant's ultimate aim and furthest goal; for many souls have no aspiration other than that.

As for what is neither praised nor blamed, it is that which is free of these two intentions and stripped of these two qualities.

The point is that this noble hadith, "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty," comprises two great principles: its beginning is knowledge (ma'rifah) and its end is conduct (sulūk). So He is known, glorified is He, by the beauty to which nothing is comparable, and He is worshipped by the beauty He loves in words, deeds and character. He loves that His servant beautify his tongue with truthfulness, his heart with sincerity, love, turning back (to Him) and reliance, his limbs with obedience, and his body by displaying His blessings upon him in his clothing, and by purifying it of impurities, ritual impurities, filth, unwanted hair, what is disliked, circumcision and trimming the nails. So He is known by attributes of beauty, and He makes Himself known through beautiful deeds, words and character; thus He is known by the beauty that is His attribute, and worshipped by the beauty that is His law and religion.

Thus the hadith combines the two principles: knowledge and conduct.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 76, verse 28:

﴿We created them and strengthened their frame﴾. This is the first creation (al-nash'ah al-ula).

Then he said: ﴿And if We wish, We can replace them with their likes, a [complete] replacement﴾. This is the other creation (al-nash'ah al-ukhra).

A parallel to this is ﴿And that He created the two mates, the male and the female, from a sperm-drop when it is emitted, and that upon Him is the other creation﴾.

This occurs very frequently in the Qur'an: it pairs the two creations, reminding natural disposition (al-fitar) and minds of one over the other. And success is from God.

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿wa-shadadna asrahum﴾ means "their creation."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-asr is the intensity of creation; one says "a horse of strong asr" (fras shadid al-asr).

He said: "Everything you bind with a saddle-strap or other such thing is ma'sur (bound)."

Al-Mubarrad said: al-asr is all strength.

Al-Layth said: "al-Asr is the strength of the joints and the articulations. 'God strengthened the asr of so-and-so' means He strengthened his creation. Everything whose two ends are gathered, so that one is bound to the other, has been asara."

Al-Hasan said: "We bound their joints to one another with the veins and sinews."

Mujahid said: it is al-sharj, meaning the place of urine and excrement; when the filth is expelled, it is contracted (tuqbadan).

(Benefit)

He also said in (al-Tibyan):

In His saying ﴿And if We wish, We replace their likes with a replacement﴾: if We wish, We destroy them and bring others resembling them, so We make them a replacement for them.

Al-Mahdawi said: a people conforming to them in creation but differing from them in deeds.

(Section)

The Creator, glory be to Him, secured the location of the liver and placed it by binding it to the stomach and all the intestines with veins, and with the membrane stretched over the abdomen that holds them all together. He connected it with ligaments from all directions. Its binding membrane connects to the diaphragm with a strong ligament, and the ligament of the liver to the diaphragm is firm and solid, because the liver is suspended from it. It is harder than the membrane of the liver, due to the great need for its firmness, since it protects the liver and the hollow vein. If a calamity strikes it, the animal dies, just as the branches of a tree perish when a calamity strikes its trunk.

He made the thinnest of these ligaments at the back, for strength with the bones, and the thickest at the front, where there are no bones to protect it. This is from the strength of the binding (al-asr) about which God the Exalted said ﴿We created them and strengthened their frame﴾.

He bound their joints with firm ligaments and made their creation connected part to part.

Since the diaphragm is a noble organ of the soul, it is given support by the two adjacent organs, the stomach and the liver, in the measure of its need, lest they crowd it and hinder it from its function; so the stomach is kept away from it by the length of its passage.

((Part Twenty-One))
